note: What the console does not implement, and why. `codes` holds the `error` codes the server can emit that no screen branches on; `endpoints` holds the public-contract endpoints no screen calls. contract/error-codes.json is the server's half of the first, rendered from internal/api's syntax tree; src/api/error-codes.ts is the console's. scripts/check-contract.mjs requires every served code and every declared endpoint to be handled or listed here, so this file is the only place either may go unimplemented — and it costs a name and a reason to put one here. An entry that stops being true — a code the server no longer emits, an endpoint a screen started calling — fails the check: this list cannot rot quietly.

codes.reason: Emitted only on listeners the console never calls. The console speaks to the console listener alone (D19, and the mount table proves it) — the PEP surface belongs to workloads holding client credentials, and the callback surface to the IdP's redirect and to external systems pushing events. A code that cannot arrive is not a code to word, and wording one would be writing copy for a screen that can never render it.

Answered by the status rather than by the code. src/api/client.ts turns 401 into a re-login the shell offers, and reports the rest as the failure they are; none of the three says anything a screen would word differently from what the status already means — the session is gone, the engine is failing, the subsystem is not installed in this deployment.

The server's own sentence is the most accurate one available, and the console shows it. These refusals arrive on surfaces the console does call, and each carries a specific message written where the rule lives — which quorum is unsatisfiable, which floor a revision breaks, which capability is missing. A console-side rewording would be a second copy of that text, maintained apart from the rule it describes, and it would drift. The generic branch renders `message` verbatim, so nothing is lost by not naming these.

Recognised by its payload rather than by its code. The dry run answers a policy that will not decode with a `diagnostics` array of pointer/code/message triples, and the builder's job is to hang each one on the field that caused it — so what it keys off is the array, in src/builder/diagnostics.ts, and the code beside it adds nothing a screen would do differently. Worth writing down rather than leaving implicit: it is the one refusal on this API the console identifies by shape, and that is why the code looks unhandled when it is not.

endpoints.name: delay-cancel
endpoints.reason: R2's delegated cancellation of a delay. The server side is finished — the endpoint, the per-authority budget, the 429 with Retry-After and the cancellation_rate_limited audit reason (decision-api 1.8.0) — and no console screen calls it, so none of that renders anywhere. Building the screen is a new feature; deleting the endpoint is a wire change on a surface other clients can already reach. Documented under `## 콘솔이 부르지 않는 표면` in docs/contracts/decision-api.md, which internal/release compares against this list.

endpoints.name: governance-lock
endpoints.reason: Turning quorum governance on is a one-time bootstrap act, and its refusal code says why the console stays out of it: `403 bootstrap_token_required`. That token is held by whoever runs the deployment, not by a console session, and carrying it into a browser to save one click would put the credential that installs governance into the place with the largest attack surface.

endpoints.name: policy-apply
endpoints.reason: The file-authoring path (U19): a policy set applied from files, which is the git-and-CI workflow's door. The console's builder changes policy through revision proposals instead — `revision-preview`, `revision-submit`, `revision-withdraw` — because a proposal is what a quorum can approve and a file apply is not.

endpoints.name: policy-export
endpoints.reason: The other half of the file-authoring path: the policy set rendered back out as files. Its caller is the CLI or CI job that keeps a repository in step with a deployment, not a screen.

endpoints.name: schema-read
endpoints.reason: The schema in force. The builder starts every draft from an empty schema and authors declarations into it, so it never reads the one already installed — which also means it cannot show an author what is in force before they replace it. That is a gap rather than a decision, and naming it here is how it stops being invisible.
